article_title: An AI-supported E-mentoring model to develop EFL pre-service teachers' self-efficacy and emotional intelligence
citation: Ismael I, Luo X and Li S (2026). An AI-supported E-mentoring model to develop EFL pre-service teachers' self-efficacy and emotional intelligence. Front. Psychol. 17:1853510. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1853510
title: Teachers' Sense of Efficacy Scale (TSES, 24-item long form) as the self-efficacy measure
description: The study used the TSES long form to measure self-efficacy across classroom management, student engagement, and instructional practices: 'The long form of the scale used in this study consists of 24 items, divided equally across these three dimensions, with responses provided on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = Nothing, 5 = A Great Deal)'. In this sample, 'Reliability coefficients ranged from 0.84 to 0.90 (α) and 0.85 to 0.91 (ω) at pre-test, and from 0.88 to 0.96 (α) and 0.89 to 0.96 (ω) at post-test'.
requirements: Administered twice, pre- and post-intervention, with approximately 1 hour for response
constraints: Administered in original English form without translation, justified by participants' advanced English proficiency
target_learning_goals: measuring perceived efficacy in classroom management, student engagement, and instructional practices
examples: Pre- and post-administration allowed measurement of change across the three teaching domains over the 10-week program
key_sources: Ismael I, Luo X and Li S (2026). An AI-supported E-mentoring model to develop EFL pre-service teachers' self-efficacy and emotional intelligence. Front. Psychol. 17:1853510. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1853510

article_title: Temporal Smoothness Doubly Robust Learning for Debiased Knowledge Tracing
citation: Peilin Zhan, Wei Chen, Weilin Chen, Shuyi Pan, Ruichu Cai. (2026). Temporal Smoothness Doubly Robust Learning for Debiased Knowledge Tracing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05958
title: Temporal Smoothness Doubly Robust (TSDR) framework for debiased knowledge tracing
description: TSDR is a model-agnostic debiasing framework for knowledge tracing that integrates a doubly robust estimator — combining Inverse Propensity Weighting with error imputation — with a temporal smoothness regularizer on the imputation model's latent trajectory. The article states that "TSDR jointly optimizes the KT predictor and the imputation model with a smoothness regularizer, effectively reducing variance while preserving the unbiasedness guarantee of DR." It treats each time step's knowledge state as a temporal "user" and co-optimizes propensity, imputation, and KT models via an alternating strategy. The smoothness constraint is motivated by the Power Law of Practice, characterizing skill acquisition as a smooth power-function trajectory.
requirements: A propensity model and an error imputation model trained jointly with the KT backbone via the alternating procedure of Algorithm 1
A smoothness coefficient lambda controlling the strength of the temporal smoothness regularization
constraints: The joint optimization of auxiliary modules incurs additional training overhead, though the article states this cost is confined to the offline phase and does not compromise online inference efficiency
target_learners: students interacting with intelligent tutoring and adaptive learning systems
target_learning_goals: accurate estimation of students' dynamic knowledge states for predicting future question mastery
examples: Applied as a plug-and-play module to six KT backbones (DKT, AKT, simpleKT, FoLiBiKT, SparseKT, DisKT) on nine real-world benchmark datasets
key_sources: Peilin Zhan, Wei Chen, Weilin Chen, Shuyi Pan, Ruichu Cai. (2026). Temporal Smoothness Doubly Robust Learning for Debiased Knowledge Tracing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05958

article_title: The Teacher’s Invisible Hand: A Meta-Analysis of the Relevance of Teacher–Student Relationship Quality for Peer Relationships and the Contribution of Student Behavior
citation: Endedijk, H. M., Breeman, L. D., van Lissa, C. J., Hendrickx, M. M. H. G., den Boer, L., & Mainhard, T. (2022). The Teacher's Invisible Hand: A Meta-Analysis of the Relevance of Teacher–Student Relationship Quality for Peer Relationships and the Contribution of Student Behavior. Review of Educational Research, 92(3), 370–412. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211051428
title: Three-mechanism framework linking teacher–student relationships to peer relationships: attachment, social learning, and social referencing
description: The article organizes explanations of how teacher–student relationship quality affects peer relationships around three theoretical mechanisms. It states that "The most prominent mechanisms that have been put forward in previous research are rooted in attachment theory, social learning theory, and social referencing theory." Attachment theory treats the teacher as a secure base and safe haven; social learning theory casts the teacher as a model whose behavior students copy with peers; social referencing theory holds that peers read teacher–student interactions as information for evaluating the student. The article notes the first two locate learning in the student, whereas social referencing locates the effect in peers' perceptions.
requirements: A teacher occupying a central social position in the classroom whose interactions with individual students are observable to peers
constraints: The framework is a theoretical account; the meta-analysis tests associations, not the mechanisms themselves
target_learners: students in preschool, primary, and secondary education (ages 3–18)
target_learning_goals: social skill development and peer relationship formation
examples: The article's Figure 1 depicts the theoretical model of the association between teacher–student and peer relationships, with student behavior as a contributing factor

The Teacher's Invisible Hand: A Meta-Analysis of the Relevance of Teacher–Student Relationship Quality for Peer Relationships and the Contribution of Student Behavior. article_title: Teacher Self-Efficacy and Its Effects on Classroom Processes, Student Academic Adjustment, and Teacher Well-Being
citation: M. Zee, H.M.Y. Koomen. (2016). Teacher self-efficacy and its effects on classroom processes, student academic adjustment, and teacher well-being: A synthesis of 40 years of research. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315626801
title: Teacher self-efficacy as an organizing framework for classroom processes, student adjustment, and teacher well-being
description: Teacher self-efficacy (TSE) serves as this review's organizing framework: the authors integrate "40 years of teacher self-efficacy (TSE) research" to map the consequences of TSE for three outcome domains — the quality of classroom processes, students' academic adjustment, and teachers' psychological well-being. Within the framework, TSE is positioned as a teacher-level belief variable positively linked to classroom quality practices and well-being factors and negatively linked to burnout, with indirect paths through instructional support and classroom organization.
constraints: The review discusses "gaps in the measurement and analysis of TSE in the educational literature".
target_learning_goals: quality of classroom processes
students' academic adjustment
teachers' psychological well-being
examples: A criteria-based review of 165 eligible articles integrating 40 years of TSE research
key_sources: M. Zee, H.M.Y. Koomen. (2016). Teacher self-efficacy and its effects on classroom processes, student academic adjustment, and teacher well-being: A synthesis of 40 years of research. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315626801

article_title: Freely available, online videos to support neurological physiotherapists and students in task-specific training skill acquisition: a scoping review.
citation: Towersey Nicola C.M., Sasse Kelvin, Stavric Verna, Alder Gemma, Saywell Nicola L. (2024). Freely available, online videos to support neurological physiotherapists and students in task-specific training skill acquisition: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05545-5
title: Task-specific training framework of six key components for motor learning
description: The review organises its content assessment around six agreed key components of task-specific training for motor learning: practice structure, specificity, repetition, modification, progression, and feedback. The article defines TST as involving "goal directed practice, repetition, progressive challenge, and positive reinforcement to optimise motor learning". Each component was assessed in the included videos for whether demonstration and/or instruction was provided, forming the basis of the 0–12 suitability scoring system.
requirements: Assessment of a TST learning resource requires evaluating whether each of the six components is present via demonstration and/or instruction
constraints: The scoring system was developed by the authors for this review, was subjective, and may have been affected by observer bias
target_learning_goals: skill acquisition of task-specific training in neurological rehabilitation
examples: The ten included videos were each scored 0–2 on the six components for a total possible score of 12, with 0–4 unsuitable, 5–8 moderately suitable and 9–12 very suitable
key_sources: Towersey Nicola C.M., Sasse Kelvin, Stavric Verna, Alder Gemma, Saywell Nicola L. (2024). Freely available, online videos to support neurological physiotherapists and students in task-specific training skill acquisition: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05545-5

article_title: Freely available, online videos to support neurological physiotherapists and students in task-specific training skill acquisition: a scoping review.
citation: Towersey Nicola C.M., Sasse Kelvin, Stavric Verna, Alder Gemma, Saywell Nicola L. (2024). Freely available, online videos to support neurological physiotherapists and students in task-specific training skill acquisition: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05545-5
title: Pragmatic 0–12 scoring rubric for assessing TST video suitability
description: A pragmatic scoring system developed for this scoping review after reviewing pertinent literature and seeking expert opinion, because no existing scoring system was appropriate. It evaluates video content against the six key TST components, scoring "0 to 2 for each of the six TST components for a total possible score of 12": 2 if both demonstration and instruction were provided, 1 for either one, 0 for a missing component. Scores of 0–4 were considered unsuitable, 5–8 moderately suitable, and 9–12 very suitable.
requirements: Assessment by raters with clinical and teaching experience in neurological physiotherapy
Independent dual assessment to reduce observer bias
constraints: The tool was developed by the authors, was subjective, and was not standardised or validated
target_learning_goals: critically evaluating the educational quality of TST video content
examples: Applied to ten included videos by two physiotherapist authors, yielding scores from 6 to 9/12
key_sources: Towersey Nicola C.M., Sasse Kelvin, Stavric Verna, Alder Gemma, Saywell Nicola L. (2024). Freely available, online videos to support neurological physiotherapists and students in task-specific training skill acquisition: a scoping review. article_title: Training technical or non-technical skills: an arbitrary distinction? A scoping review.
citation: Gamborg ML, Salling LB, Rölfing JD, Jensen RD. (2024). Training technical or non-technical skills: an arbitrary distinction? A scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06419-6
title: TS and NTS as interrelated constructs whose separation in learning designs may be arbitrary
description: The review proposes that technical and non-technical skills are interrelated constructs rather than independent categories, based on the pattern that "the results strongly indicate a correlation between TS and NTS skills, suggesting that physicians who are proficient in their NTS, also perform well on their TS." It frames the conventional split in learning designs as possibly arbitrary, drawing on socio-cultural educational studies, motor learning accounts in which motor control results from continuous cognitive adaptation, Gibson's affordances, and self-regulated learning frameworks such as Zimmerman's circular model and Ziegler's actiotope model.
requirements: Future studies should simultaneously assess both skill sets to establish how improvement in TS is influenced by NTS and vice versa
constraints: The supporting socio-cultural studies were qualitative and cannot establish whether a clear relationship between TS and NTS exists
Quantitative studies in the review lacked theoretical presentation or discussion of how TS and NTS interact
target_learners: healthcare professionals and physicians in medical education
target_learning_goals: integration of technical and non-technical clinical skills
examples: The review cites Cleland et al. and Tsuda et al. as showing acquisition of TS happens in relation to other learners and teachers, and quotes Gibson (1979, p. 223): "we must perceive in order to move, but we must also move in order to perceive."
key_sources: Gamborg ML, Salling LB, Rölfing JD, Jensen RD. (2024). Training technical or non-technical skills: an arbitrary distinction? A scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06419-6

article_title: Impact of the Teacher Study Group Professional Development Program on Student Vocabulary and Observed Teaching Practice: A Replication in First Grade Classrooms
citation: Russell Gersten, Joseph Dimino, Madhavi Jayanthi, Rebecca Newman-Gonchar, Mary Jo Taylor. (2013). Impact of the Teacher Study Group Professional Development Program on Student Vocabulary and Observed Teaching Practice: A Replication in First Grade Classrooms. SREE Spring 2013 Conference Abstract. http://www2.ed.gov/policy/elsec/leg/blueprint
title: Teacher Study Group (TSG) professional development program with facilitator's guide and five-phase session process
description: The TSG intervention is a concentrated professional development effort to improve first grade teachers' vocabulary teaching practice and student vocabulary outcomes. It consists of 11 interactive twice-monthly school-site sessions of approximately 75 minutes, covering topics such as Words in Context, Selecting Words to Teach, and Student Friendly Definitions. Each session follows a five-phase recursive process: Debrief, Discuss the Focus Research Concept, Compare the Focus Research Concept with Practice, Plan Collaboratively, and Assignment. Facilitators use the TSG facilitator's guide providing a specific "game plan" and attend a 2-day training with ongoing support.
requirements: Sessions are facilitated by literacy personnel from each school who attend a 2-day training and receive ongoing support as needed, using the facilitator's guide
target_learners: first grade teachers in Title I schools
target_learning_goals: effective vocabulary instruction
integrating research-based instructional strategies into existing curriculum
examples: In the replication, 94 treatment teachers participated in TSG sessions facilitated by school literacy personnel across 31 Title I schools in four states
key_sources: Russell Gersten, Joseph Dimino, Madhavi Jayanthi, Rebecca Newman-Gonchar, Mary Jo Taylor. (2013). Impact of the Teacher Study Group Professional Development Program on Student Vocabulary and Observed Teaching Practice: A Replication in First Grade Classrooms. SREE Spring 2013 Conference Abstract. http://www2.ed.gov/policy/elsec/leg/blueprint

article_title: Impact of the Teacher Study Group Professional Development Program on Student Vocabulary and Observed Teaching Practice: A Replication in First Grade Classrooms
citation: Russell Gersten, Joseph Dimino, Madhavi Jayanthi, Rebecca Newman-Gonchar, Mary Jo Taylor. (2013). Impact of the Teacher Study Group Professional Development Program on Student Vocabulary and Observed Teaching Practice: A Replication in First Grade Classrooms. SREE Spring 2013 Conference Abstract. http://www2.ed.gov/policy/elsec/leg/blueprint
title: Effective professional development should orchestrate linkage to core curriculum, concreteness, collegial networks, and ongoing activities into a feasible school model
description: The article presents the Teacher Study Group as an attempt to orchestrate several of the "best practices" in professional development into a feasible model for elementary schools. These practices are linkage to core curriculum, concreteness, establishment of collegial networks, and ongoing related activities. The goal is to enhance instruction by helping teachers integrate research-based instructional strategies into their existing curriculum rather than delivering decontextualized training.
requirements: Sessions must be ongoing, job-embedded, and linked to the core curriculum and school needs
constraints: The article notes such advocated approaches have rarely been widely field-tested and evaluated using rigorous research techniques, and results have often been mixed
target_learning_goals: research-based vocabulary and comprehension instruction
examples: TSG sessions were held at the school site twice a month before or after school to maximize instructional time, with teachers collaboratively planning and then implementing lessons between sessions

article_title: Affordable Online Maths Tuition: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Carole Torgerson, Hannah Ainsworth, Hannah Buckley, Gillen Hampden-Thompson, Catherine Hewitt, Deborah Humphry, Laura Jefferson, Natasha Mitchell, David Torgerson. (2016). Affordable Online Maths Tuition: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Third Space Learning Affordable Maths Tuition programme
description: An "online one to one numeracy programme designed to support children in Key Stage 2", delivered by Third Space Learning with tutors who are maths graduates in India and Sri Lanka. Pupils receive weekly 45-minute one-to-one sessions during the school day in a secure virtual classroom, with the same tutor each week, headsets, and a shared virtual whiteboard. Teachers select lessons from a curriculum of 274 lessons to target individual learning gaps, and tutors provide detailed session reporting. In the evaluation it was delivered over 27 weeks from September 2014 to May 2015 at a cost of £378 per pupil.
requirements: A reliable internet connection and a designated space for online tuition sessions, as specified in the school agreement to participate
Teacher time to create pupil academic profiles, select weekly lessons, and a teaching assistant to supervise sessions
constraints: In this evaluation schools did not pay the full cost, and TSL normally would not specify the length of time a pupil takes part
The evaluation occurred when TSL was in an initial testing phase working with 70 schools
target_learners: Year 6 primary pupils predicted to achieve KS2 level 3 or an insecure level 4 in maths
target_learning_goals: Maths skills in the final year of primary school, targeting learning gaps arising in class
examples: In the trial, 64 schools were randomised and 600 identified pupils were offered weekly sessions; compliance was summarised from TSL session data
key_sources: Carole Torgerson, Hannah Ainsworth, Hannah Buckley, Gillen Hampden-Thompson, Catherine Hewitt, Deborah Humphry, Laura Jefferson, Natasha Mitchell, David Torgerson. (2016). Affordable Online Maths Tuition: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581116

article_title: Using Blended Learning in Developing Student Teachers Teaching Skills
citation: Isman, A., Abanmy, F. A., Hussein, H. B., & Al Saadany, M. A. (2012). Using Blended Learning in Developing Student Teachers Teaching Skills. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 11(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1000130
title: Teaching Skills Scale Card (TSSC) for observing student teachers' teaching implementation skills
description: The Teaching Skills Scale Card (TSSC) is an observation instrument prepared by the authors in 2011 for rating student teachers' teaching implementation skills during classroom observation. It covers four domains — planning (13 points), learning strategies and classroom management (28 points), knowledge of subject matter (20 points), and evaluation (14 points) — for a total score of 75, with each standard operationalized by concrete behavioral indicators such as "Uses dialogue as a means of knowing the needs and experience of students."
requirements: Requires classroom observation of student teachers by trained raters using the card's behavioral indicators
constraints: Developed for the field education context at Teachers College, King Saud University
target_learning_goals: teaching implementation skills including planning, classroom management, subject knowledge, and evaluation
examples: Used with pre-post application to observe student teachers in classrooms in the four experimental groups
key_sources: Isman, A., Abanmy, F. A., Hussein, H. B., & Al Saadany, M. A. (2012). Using Blended Learning in Developing Student Teachers Teaching Skills. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 11(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ989298

article_title: Psychological predictors of professional readiness: modeling the effects of preservice teachers' 21st-century skills on self-efficacy and professional attitudes.
citation: Serçe Hüseyin, Aydoğmuş Mevlüt, Şentürk Cihad. (2026). Psychological predictors of professional readiness: modeling the effects of preservice teachers' 21st-century skills on self-efficacy and professional attitudes. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-05039-7
title: Teacher Self-Efficacy Perception Scale-Short Form (TSES-SF)
description: The Teachers' Sense of Efficacy Scale–Short Form, originally developed by Tschannen-Moran and Woolfolk Hoy and adapted into Turkish, consists of "12 items grouped into three factors": self-efficacy in student engagement, instructional strategies, and classroom management, rated on a nine-point Likert scale. In this study CFA verified the three-factor structure (CFI = 0.97, RMSEA = 0.077) and subscale alphas ranged from 0.74 to 0.80.
requirements: Nine-point Likert response format from 1 (not at all) to 9 (a great deal)
target_learning_goals: assessment of teacher self-efficacy across engagement, instructional strategies, and classroom management
examples: Served as the teacher self-efficacy outcome measure in the structural model

article_title: External validity of task-specific metrics for performance assessment in laparoscopic crural repair.
citation: Garces-Palacios S, Desir A, Pise A, Holcomb C, Scott DJ, Sankaranarayanan G. (2026). External validity of task-specific metrics for performance assessment in laparoscopic crural repair. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-026-12767-9
title: Task-specific metrics (TSMs) for laparoscopic crural repair assessment
description: A structured assessment instrument developed via hierarchical task analysis of the laparoscopic hiatal hernia procedure, systematically deconstructing it into discrete tasks, sub-tasks, and motor actions. Domains include procedural technique (suture placement, crural re-approximation), general laparoscopic skills (bimanual dexterity, flow of operation), and tissue handling, with items scored 0, 3, or 5 points. This study evaluated its external validity in an international cohort.
requirements: Video-recorded performances for independent blinded assessment by trained raters
constraints: Developed and validated for simulated crural repair using an inanimate silicone model in a laparoscopic trainer box
target_learning_goals: technical performance in laparoscopic crural repair
procedural knowledge
tissue handling
examples: Applied to 30 video-recorded simulated crural repairs at the 2024 SAGES Annual Meeting
key_sources: Garces-Palacios S, Desir A, Pise A, Holcomb C, Scott DJ, Sankaranarayanan G. (2026). External validity of task-specific metrics for performance assessment in laparoscopic crural repair. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-026-12767-9

article_title: Benchmarking LLM chatbots' oncological knowledge with the Turkish Society of Medical Oncology's annual board examination questions.
citation: Cem, E. E., & Eren, K. E. (2025). Benchmarking LLM chatbots’ oncological knowledge with the Turkish Society of Medical Oncology’s annual board examination questions. BMC Cancer. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12885-025-13596-0
title: Turkish Society of Medical Oncology board examination benchmark: 790 Turkish-language multiple-choice questions from eight annual exams (2016–2024)
description: A benchmark of 790 valid multiple-choice questions drawn from eight annual Turkish Society of Medical Oncology board examinations between 2016 and 2024, each with a single correct answer and categorized into oncology topics such as "Basic oncology, epidemiology and statistics" (118 questions). Questions were kept in Turkish with grammatical errors uncorrected, and a passing score of 50 correct answers was used. The datasets generated are stated to be available in the appendix.
requirements: Permission to use the examination questions was obtained from the Turkish Society of Medical Oncology
Questions were edited only to eliminate typos and unintentional punctuation, remaining in Turkish
constraints: The 2020 exam was not conducted due to the COVID-19 pandemic, so eight exams yield 800 questions of which 790 were valid after excluding canceled questions
target_learners: medical oncologists and oncology trainees preparing for board examinations
target_learning_goals: oncological knowledge across subspecialties including basic oncology, tumor types, and palliative care
examples: Each model answered questions in separate Turkish-language chat sessions beginning with the prompt "I will give you some multiple-choice questions with one correct answer; you will tell me your answers"
key_sources: Cem, E. E., & Eren, K. E. (2025). Benchmarking LLM chatbots’ oncological knowledge with the Turkish Society of Medical Oncology’s annual board examination questions. BMC Cancer. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12885-025-13596-0

article_title: The Quest for Comparability: Studying the Invariance of the Teachers' Sense of Self-Efficacy (TSES) Measure across Countries.
citation: Scherer, R., Jansen, M., Nilsen, T., Areepattamannil, S., & Marsh, H. W. (2016). The Quest for Comparability: Studying the Invariance of the Teachers' Sense of Self-Efficacy (TSES) Measure across Countries. PLoS ONE, 11(3), e0150829. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0150829
title: Multidimensional framework of teachers' self-efficacy: classroom management, instruction, and student engagement
description: Following Tschannen-Moran and Woolfolk Hoy, the article describes teachers' self-efficacy as comprising three related but distinct facets aligned with specific teaching practices. "Self-efficacy in classroom management refers to their capabilities for establishing an orderly environment without disruptions and coping with disruptive behavior"; self-efficacy in instruction concerns the use of alternative teaching practices, assessment strategies, and explanations; and self-efficacy in student engagement addresses emotional and cognitive support for students, including capabilities to motivate students for learning. The TSES scale operationalises these three factors, each with four items in the TALIS 2013 short form.
requirements: Measurement should account for the interrelated yet disparate nature of the three factors, including potential conceptual overlap between facets
constraints: The article notes the three aspects of teaching "are not strictly distinct", so items may not be exclusively related to one factor
target_learning_goals: understanding and measuring teachers' beliefs in their capabilities to enact teaching behaviour that influences student outcomes
examples: TALIS 2013 asked teachers to rate four statements per factor on a four-point scale (1 = not at all, 4 = a lot)
key_sources: Scherer, R., Jansen, M., Nilsen, T., Areepattamannil, S., & Marsh, H. W. (2016). The Quest for Comparability: Studying the Invariance of the Teachers' Sense of Self-Efficacy (TSES) Measure across Countries. PLoS ONE, 11(3), e0150829. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0150829

article_title: Evaluation of effectiveness of instruction and study habits in two consecutive clinical semesters of the medical curriculum Munich (MeCuM) reveals the need for more time for self study and higher frequency of assessment.
citation: Mueller Sophia, Weichert Nina, Stoecklein Veit, Hammitzsch Ariane, Pascuito Giulia, Krug Christian, Holzer Matthias, Pfeiffer Mona, Siebeck Matthias, Schmidmaier Ralf. (2011). Evaluation of effectiveness of instruction and study habits in two consecutive clinical semesters of the medical curriculum munich (MeCuM) reveals the need for more time for self study and higher frequency of assessment. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-11-62
title: TSS/QI ratio as a parameter for effectiveness of instruction
description: The article adopts the ratio of time spent on self-study (TSS) to quantity of instruction (QI), following Gijselaers and Schmidt and the time-on-task hypothesis, as a measurable parameter of instructional effectiveness. A TSS/QI of three means that for every hour of instruction students spend three hours on self-study. The article states that "TSS/QI has been shown to positively correlate with achievement and can therefore be considered a parameter for effective instruction", and uses it to evaluate the MeCuM clinical semesters.
requirements: Requires weekly measurement of students' self-study time and mandatory lesson quantity, as done via the weekly anonymous questionnaires
constraints: The article notes this study did not demonstrate the impact of TSS on learning outcome, and that the measure concerns quantity of instruction, not quality
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in clinical semesters
target_learning_goals: effective use of self-study time for learning clinical medicine
examples: The ratio was calculated weekly for four surgical and four internal medicine semesters, using 1,976 and 1,277 complete TSS/QI pairs respectively
key_sources: Mueller Sophia, Weichert Nina, Stoecklein Veit, Hammitzsch Ariane, Pascuito Giulia, Krug Christian, Holzer Matthias, Pfeiffer Mona, Siebeck Matthias, Schmidmaier Ralf. (2011). Evaluation of effectiveness of instruction and study habits in two consecutive clinical semesters of the medical curriculum munich (MeCuM) reveals the need for more time for self study and higher frequency of assessment. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-11-62
